paras: The attempted lynching of Charley Wilson took place near Mhoon's Landing, Mississippi, on the night of August 29, 1900, when a band of men hunting an accused murderer put a noose around the neck of Wilson, a Black man from Greenville. The men released him when they noticed a scar on his face that the man they sought did not have. The dispatch circulated widely in the white press as a story of mistaken identity, and the Kansas City American Citizen reported it twice.

The search followed the killing of Tom Mike, a levee contractor, near Mhoon's Landing. The men were looking for Dick Johnson, whom the Associated Press version called "the alleged murderer" and the longer version simply "the murderer."

The band caught Wilson near the landing, and according to the longer dispatch his "resemblance to Johnson was so close" that the men prepared to hang him on the spot. They swung a rope over the limb of a tree and put the noose around his neck, and ten men took hold of the rope. At that point someone saw that Wilson had a scar on his face that Johnson lacked, and the men let him go. The longer version added that "further investigations showed that he was an innocent man."
No report of any arrest of the men, of an inquiry, or of Johnson's capture appears in the coverage.

White papers from Louisville and Birmingham to Indiana, Ohio, Nebraska, Kansas, Kentucky, Illinois and South Dakota ran the dispatch between August 30 and September 1. Their headlines treated it as a narrow escape or a curiosity, such as "Saved by a Scar," "Close Call" and "Saved at the Last Moment," or stressed the error, as in "Had the Wrong Negro" and "Almost Hung the Wrong Negro." The Louisville Courier-Journal's fuller text called the men "lynchers" and described them as about to swing Wilson "into eternity," but offered no comment on their conduct.

The American Citizen of Kansas City printed the Associated Press text on its third page under the headline "Negro About to Be Lynched When It Is Discovered He Is the Wrong Man." On its front page, the same issue carried its own brief, which alone identified the attackers as "a mob of white men" and said Wilson had been "swung up to a tree." That brief stood in a column beside a prediction that an accused Black man in Alabama would soon be lynched and news of a legal challenge to Southern disfranchisement laws.

The wire texts say the men were about to hang Wilson when the scar was noticed, while the American Citizen's brief says he had already been swung up, and only that brief gives the race of the men. The Birmingham Age-Herald named the slain contractor "Tom Pike" rather than Tom Mike.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Charley Wilson
bases: A band of about ten men hunting an accused murderer put a noose around Charley Wilson's neck and prepared to hang him before releasing him on finding he was the wrong man, an attempted lynching (A1, A3, A6).

Wilson was released alive, so no killing occurred (A1, A3, A6); the band of ten men acted without lawful authority to punish the alleged murder of a contractor, which makes this an attempted lynching rather than a lynching (A1, A4).

Every report, white and Black, traces to a single press dispatch from Mhoon's Landing in a longer and a shorter (Associated Press) form (A1, A4, A7); the American Citizen's own brief adds only that the men were white and that Wilson was 'swung up' (A6), and no local or independent account was found.

accounts.label: Wire report, longer version
accounts.gist: Wilson 'came within an inch of paying with his life' for Mike's murder; his resemblance to Johnson led ten men to noose him, the scar stayed 'the hands of the lynchers', and investigation showed he was innocent.

accounts.label: Wire report, shorter (Associated Press) version
accounts.gist: A band searching for Johnson caught Wilson, noosed him under a tree limb with ten men on the rope, and released him when the scar was noticed.

accounts.label: American Citizen brief
accounts.gist: A 'mob of white men' caught Wilson and 'swung [him] up to a tree'; he was released when it was found he was not the man wanted.

framing.detail: Papers from Louisville to South Dakota ran the dispatch under headlines stressing the lucky escape ('Saved by a Scar', 'Close Call', 'Saved at the Last Moment') or the mistake ('Had the Wrong Negro', 'Almost Hung the Wrong Negro'), without comment on the band.
The longer version used the phrase 'swinging the negro into eternity' and called the men 'lynchers', while treating Johnson as 'the murderer' without qualification.
The American Citizen reprinted the shorter wire text on page 3 under a headline naming it a near-lynching of 'the Wrong Man'.

Its page-1 brief identified the attackers as 'a mob of white men' and set the case beside a predicted Alabama lynching and Southern disfranchisement news, without explicit editorial comment on Wilson.

versions.value: Noose around his neck and ten men on the rope 'preparatory to hanging' him when the scar was noticed; not lifted
'swung up to a tree' before being released

conflicts.note: The wire text, the fuller and earlier account, describes the men as about to hang him; the American Citizen's brief condensation says he was swung up.
Only the Black-press brief names the men's race.
All other printings give 'Mike'; 'Pike' is likely a typesetting or OCR variant.
Differences in wording between the two wire versions.
All fit the night of Wednesday, Aug. 29; later datelines (Aug. 30, 31) belong to reprints.

Near Mhoon's Landing (also printed Moon's Landing, Mohans Landing)
Charley (Charles) Wilson, a Black man ('negro', 'colored man') from Greenville, Miss.
Wilson himself was not accused; the band was hunting Dick Johnson, 'the alleged murderer' of levee contractor Tom Mike, and took Wilson for Johnson because of a close resemblance
